title: Why Conway favoured an immediate New Zealand rate rise despite weak household spending
summary: Paul Conway put his disagreement with October’s decision in terms of timing. The Monetary Policy Committee voted four to three to hold the official cash rate at 2.75%. He preferred a 25 basis point increase to 3%. Speaking in his individual capacity on 10 November, he explained why a supply shock could warrant tighter policy even while the recovery had yet to reach many households. Prolonged cost increases could change price-setting behaviour, leaving the committee facing a larger or longer tightening later. Members broadly agreed that a further increase would probably be necessary, conditional on the outlook. They differed over the cost of waiting for evidence (speaking notes, slides 1–3).

The majority saw room to wait. September-quarter inflation undershot expectations; wage growth, margins and measures of expected inflation gave some reassurance. Two earlier increases of 25 basis points each were still working through the economy, household demand was weak and global risks were material. Conway attached greater weight to the spread of inflation across the consumption basket. Annual headline inflation fell from 4.1% in June to 3.7% in September. Yet the share of items with annual price increases around or above 3% rose from 40% to 55%. On slide 9 the bars measure breadth on the left axis, while the line records annual CPI on the right. A lower headline reading could therefore coexist with rapid price increases across a larger share of the basket. The 4.4% figure for the December quarter on slide 5 was a projection conditioned on oil futures at the time of the review (slides 3–9).

Conway also drew attention to what firms expected to do next. A net 48% expected to raise prices in the three months before Christmas. This survey balance measures intentions, not the size of any price rise. He saw five- and ten-year inflation expectations above the 2% midpoint, while acknowledging that various measures gave a mixed picture and the cited survey was due for an update. Weak sales had limited some firms’ ability to pass on costs. Stable profit margins could nevertheless coexist with inflation if firms kept selling prices rising with input costs. These considerations led him to take the persistence risk seriously even though domestic non-tradables inflation had been easing (slides 6, 10–11).

Export strength made it plausible to him that the economy could absorb another increase. Strong commodity prices, higher export volumes and tourism supported activity. Export earnings were feeding into business investment. Households presented a different picture: consumption was flat in the June quarter, aggregate income gains outpaced spending and some households were repaying debt. Weak employment growth and subdued housing prices in parts of the North Island restricted the recovery. A lower New Zealand dollar helped exporters and tourism while also raising import costs and the domestic price of goods that could be sold abroad. Its trade-weighted fall since 2020 was around 10–15% depending on the starting date (slides 13–23).

Conway saw higher global investment demand and government borrowing as possible reasons why long yields had risen. He would infer a change in the neutral rate from the economy’s response rather than adjust the cash rate automatically to a model estimate. His preferred vote also happened to align with what he described as a largely priced-in hike. He saw little merit in surprising markets on this occasion but reserved the right to do so when justified. Between the vote and his remarks, labour-market figures had weakened, oil prices had fallen and AI-related equities abroad had sold off. Those developments illustrated the uncertainty around the next decision. They were unavailable when members cast their votes (slides 3, 24–26).

questions.question: Is broader inflation surviving the reversal in oil prices?
questions.detail: Conway identifies a rise in the share of fast-rising items even as annual headline inflation falls. For the near-term rate path, examine successive distributions of price changes within domestic services and fuel-intensive tradables, allowing for earlier price increases dropping out of annual comparisons. Stats NZ’s detailed CPI releases and the RBNZ’s range of core measures could show where sustained repricing survives a reversal of the original shock.

questions.question: Will export income translate into spending outside export-intensive regions?
questions.detail: The presentation documents a gap between disposable income and consumption and points to debt repayment. It cannot establish how much additional spending exporters, employees and suppliers will undertake. Compare subsequent regional employment, retail volumes and household debt with export receipts in areas with differing industry mixes. National accounts and official regional and lending data would help judge whether a further increase could be absorbed without a wider contraction.

questions.question: Are higher expectations becoming actual wage and pricing decisions?
questions.detail: The net balance of firms planning increases concerns the next three months, while Conway’s concern about expectations extends five and ten years ahead. Either survey can move without an equivalent change in prices. Compare the next RBNZ Survey of Expectations and business survey with realised wage settlements, selling-price changes and margins. This would help determine how much persistence to build into a short-rate view beyond the next meeting.
